title: 'Exorcising' INEC's ghost voters
excerpt: INEC removed 1,609,553 names, including 873 dead voters, from its register and will prosecute 54 staff over invalid registrations ahead of the 2027 electio
content:
Recently, what can only be described as an “administrative exorcism”, or the expulsion of the dead and the dreadful living, occurred on the Independent National Electoral Commission online portal, and Nigerians must hope there will be no recurrence of the breaches that led to the “exorcism”.

By the way, exorcism drives out, eliminates or expels spirits of the dead, evil living spirits, demons or unwanted supernatural forces from a person, place, object or organisation, with prayers that are sometimes called deliverances, sacred rites and other religious or spiritual ceremonies.

Prof Joash Amupitan announced that INEC, of which he is chairman, has removed the names of 1,609,553 voters following a clean-up of the 2025/2026 Continuous Voter Registration exercise, and that the Final Register of Voters for the 2027 General Elections will be officially published on December 15, 2026.

After being asked to confirm the veracity of information on INEC’s temporary online voters register, some members of the public were able to discover fake registrations, names of dead voters, and fake AI-generated voter photographs.

When announcing that this exercise concludes the 2025/2026 Continuous Voter Registration ahead of the 2027 General Elections, Prof Amupitan revealed that 873 of the names that were removed belonged to dead registered voters, while the balance of 1,608,660 were invalid voters.

He further disclosed that INEC has identified the 54 staff members found culpable in the invalid registration of voters and that disciplinary actions, including prosecution in court, will be taken against them.

Section 118(d) of the Electoral Act provides that “A person who makes in any record, register or document which he or she is required to prepare, publish or keep for the purpose of registration, any entry or statement which he or she knows to be false or does not believe to be true, commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a maximum fine of N500,000 or to imprisonment for a term of 12 months or both.”

Some Nigerians, who think that this penalty is too lenient, suggest that the jail term should be increased, and should not have the option of a fine. This, they argue, should serve as a deterrent to those mischievous INEC staff who may want to derail the electoral process (and Nigeria’s democracy) as enemies within.

Prof Amupitan assures Nigerians that, as a result of this breach, and to guard against such practices by its staff or others outside its operations, INEC has decided to strengthen its voter registration controls with “enhanced biometric capture, authentication and verification safeguards”.

This exercise should help INEC succeed with the integrity tests that will come when the election finally gets under way, and voters should have no cause to complain that their names were omitted, their published details are inaccurate or that a deceased voter is still listed on the Register.

If 54 members of INEC staff are mischievous or criminal-minded enough to compromise the Voters Register with more than 1.6 million phantom voters, no one can be too sure of the integrity of the registration work that the election management agency has done so far.

It is safe to assume that the conspiracy between INEC in-house personnel and their external collaborators is still very much alive and won’t go away soon. This is because of the pecuniary and hegemonic advantages of winning elections in Nigeria, where the winner always takes all.

A potentially dangerous dimension of the ability of unauthorised or disloyal personnel to compromise the INEC portal is in the recent media report that the Israeli military was able to upload about 3.5 million photographs of Palestinians, residents in Gaza, onto Amazon’s cloud platform so that the individuals can be easily identified and set up for accurate aerial bombardment to death.

It also demonstrates, without doubt, the extent to which the digital technology called Alternative Intelligence can be used to achieve almost anything, from the benign and positive to the mischievous and downright dangerous.

What has just happened demonstrates that INEC’s internal control may not be robust enough to prevent or reduce breaches. It also agrees with the prescient observation made at a recent Abuja Conference on AI by Ayo Atobatele, a computer scientist, that “election results can only be manipulated within INEC.”

Fake entries of more than 1.6 million, out of 103 million registered voters, are roughly 1.5 per cent and significant. While the criminal 54, out of nearly 15,000, INEC members of staff, may appear nominally minimal, it has formed a significant critical mass and is therefore too high and unacceptable.

INEC must evolve stricter internal administrative controls to detect and prevent future breaches. One way to achieve this is to invite consulting firms, like Deloitte, to audit its personnel recruitment mechanism, operational processes and administrative controls and make suggestions on ways to at least improve its operations and significantly reduce breaches, if it cannot eliminate them.

Because synthetically generated content can easily compromise the integrity of data on any digital portal, INEC must employ, or contract, individuals who are savvy with Artificial Intelligence to regularly scour and detect malicious attacks against its data.

Also, INEC should engage private investigators to check out its personnel who handle sensitive administrative and operational schedules to find out if there are still more officers who may be members of the syndicate that can be used by mischievous and overly ambitious politicians, who are determined to undermine the integrity of elections in Nigeria.

INEC has to do more than deny that its officials can remotely log out of the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System before the end of voting at the polling booths. Indeed, what assurances do the voters have that a polling officer, whom INEC acknowledges has the authority to log in and log out during voting, will be faithful to INEC’s instructions and values?

Is there a way for non-INEC staff to be part of the logging in and out of the BVAS as the presiding officer carries out this highly sensitive responsibility? Accountants sometimes adopt procedures that help safeguard the integrity of access to cash and sensitive documents.

They share access passwords into two or more component parts, such that it will take many officers to provide their components of a single password before a safe can be accessed or a process activated. In other words, only one officer should not be allowed to single-handedly run a security routine.

INEC should adopt this process, so that the presiding officer cannot unilaterally log in or log out of a BVAS on election day. This may appear to be a little cumbersome and maybe increase the budget, but it should help to reduce suspicion and give additional credibility to the outcome of voting on election day.

A human-driven control should justify the legal, technological and financial investment in the election management agency that is expected to deliver a free, fair, credible and verifiable election process that will drive Nigeria’s democratic values of the Fourth Republic.

This is just a roundabout way of saying that the human element in the election management process must be helped, nay, compelled, to conform to the demands and the expectations of the rule of law, on the pain of swift and full penalty for all deliberate breaches.
